newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland sees special regional role within NATO.
newsitem.headline: Poland sees special regional role within NATO.

text.p: Poland as a future NATO member, is set to play a special role in Eastern and Central Europe and take special responsibility for its stability, Foreign Minister Dariusz Rosati said on Thursday.

"Poland is the biggest country of this region...a country which is fast growing economically and one of the three invited to join NATO...all this means Poland is one of the main partners of the United States," Rosati told reporters after a meeting U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright in Warsaw.

"All this means Poland has special responsibility for stability in the whole region and maintaining good relations with its neighbours...and it is also a belief of the United States that Poland plays such a role," Rosati said.
The 16 NATO leaders in Madrid this week invited Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary to start talks on joining the pact, which they aim to enter by 1999.
Albright, who came to Warsaw with U.S. President Bill Clinton to celebrate the invitation, echoed Rosati's remarks.
"I think that we have thought for a long time Poland has a very important role in Central and Eastern Europe," she told reporters.

Poland, relatively far advanced in economic reform and on the road to integration with NATO and the European Union, has been working to act as a bridge and advocate for regional neighbours with further to go.

It has scored notable successes in overcoming historic suspicions to cooperate with Lithuania and with Ukraine, the success and independence of which both Warsaw and Western analysts view as crucial to European security.
Now its own road to NATO looks more certain, Poland is advocating that other countries should have a similar chance.

Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski, addressing Clinton before a crowd gathered on a Warsaw city square, listed examples of such countries including the Baltic states -- whose NATO entry is especially firmly opposed by Russia.
"Poland in NATO will not for a moment forget about the aspirations and hopes of Romania, Slovenia, Lithuania, Estonia, Slovakia and Bulgaria," Kwasniewski said.
He said Poland also placed great hopes in ties with Russia.
Rosati said he and Albright had swapped estimates of the costs of integration of Poland's forces into NATO and how the enlargement burden would be shared out in the alliance, but he gave no figures.
